report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-β plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau.
Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist, was previously shown to acutely reduce the ratio of phosphorylated tau-181 to unphosphorylated tau-181 (pT181/T181) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
However, its effects on plasma pT181/T181 and broader proteomic networks remain unknown.
Here, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg.
Paired CSF and plasma samples were collected longitudinally via indwelling intrathecal and intravenous catheters.
Plasma AD biomarkers were quantified by mass spectrometry, and proteomic profiling was performed using the SomaScan 11K assay on samples from hours 0, 16, and 24.
Suvorexant increased pT181/T181 in plasma while decreasing it in CSF between 08:00-16:00.

At the pathway level, suvorexant increased the extracellular abundance of proteins associated with translation, RNA binding, cytoskeletal organization and endosomal sorting, centrally at 16 hours and peripherally at 24 hours, and decreased cytokine and receptor-ligand signaling and serine protease activity in plasma at 24 hours.

As plasma biomarkers are increasingly used for clinical screening and trial enrollment, factors that influence their levels, including medications, must be identified and their effects on interpretation understood.

Alzheimer disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of extracellular amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques and intraneuronal tau tangles, leading to synaptic dysfunction, cognitive decline, and eventually death. 1 Recent advances in biofluid biomarker development have enabled increasingly sensitive and specific detection of AD pathology using blood-based markers, complementing wellestablished cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and neuroimaging modalities. 2, 3 CSF biomarkers such as Aβ42, phosphorylated tau (p-tau) and total tau (t-tau) reflect key aspects of AD pathophysiology and are widely used in both clinical and research settings.

text.text: These markers, however, require lumbar puncture and are not always feasible for large-scale or longitudinal studies.

In contrast, plasma-based biomarkers, including Aβ42 and p-tau forms, are minimally invasive and reach a level of analytical performance that allows for reliable detection of early pathological changes in AD. 4, 5 However, questions remain about the concordance and timing of changes in AD biomarkers between plasma and CSF, particularly in response to pharmacological interventions.

text.text: Aβ and tau dynamics. 6, 7 Orexins (also known as hypocretins) are hypothalamic neuropeptides that promote arousal and regulate sleep-wake transitions. 8 In animal models, orexin antagonism reduces Aβ levels and plaque formation while orexin administration increases interstitial Aβ levels. 9 Furthermore, blocking orexin also decreases tau-mediated neurodegeneration through reduced phosphorylation of tau. 10 Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA), is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of insomnia. 11 A recent randomized controlled trial in cognitively unimpaired adults demonstrated that a single dose of suvorexant 20 mg acutely reduced CSF Aβ levels approximately 10-20% and decreased the ratio of phosphorylated tau-threonine-181 to unphosphorylated tau-threonine-181 (pT181/T181), a site linked to early AD pathology, approximately 10-15% compared to placebo. 12 These changes occurred in the absence of measurable differences in total sleep time or sleep architecture, suggesting a direct pharmacodynamic effect of orexin receptor antagonism on CSF AD biomarkers.

text.text: While these results provide compelling evidence that suvorexant modulates key AD biomarkers in the central nervous system (CNS), a number of critical questions remain such as suvorexant's effect on plasma AD biomarkers, the degree to which the CNS effects translate to peripheral compartments, and the molecular breadth of suvorexant's effects.

In addition to understanding the effects of suvorexant on AD biomarkers, understanding the systems-level proteomic effects could reveal mechanistic insights into orexin modulation and inform future prevention strategies.
High-throughput proteomic technologies offer a powerful approach to characterize the broad biological effects of CNS-active agents such as suvorexant.
SomaScan, developed by SomaLogic, uses modified DNA aptamers (SOMAmers) to quantify 11,000 aptamers with high specificity and sensitivity from small-volume plasma or CSF samples.
It covers a broad range of biological processes including inflammation, synaptic function, metabolism, vascular health, and phosphorylation cascades.
Complementary to this, NUcleic acid Linked Immuno-Sandwich Assay (NULISA) is a bead-based, highsensitivity immunoassay platform optimized for low-abundance protein detection.

Together, these platforms enable accurate measurement of core AD biomarkers, deep profiling of known AD-relevant pathways, and the discovery of novel protein networks altered by suvorexant in both CSF and plasma.
This study tests the acute effect of suvorexant 20 mg on pT181/T181 and other AD biomarkers in paired CSF and plasma samples compared to placebo.
The results will establish the degree to which peripheral changes in AD biomarkers reflect central dynamics, a critical issue for blood-based diagnostic development and drug monitoring.
Then, we will determine whether suvorexant 20 mg alters individual protein levels and proteomic networks in plasma and CSF relative to placebo.
We aim to identify proteomic networks whose response to suvorexant may be compartment-specific or correlated with changes in p-tau levels.

By integrating targeted biomarkers and untargeted systems proteomics, this study aims to develop a comprehensive molecular map of suvorexant's acute effects on the human proteome in both central and peripheral compartments.

Findings from this work will inform both the utility of suvorexant as a repurposed diseasemodifying therapeutic and the development of fluid biomarkers for early pharmacodynamic effects in prevention trials.

This study found that suvorexant increases plasma pT181/T181 and peaks approximately 15 hours post-dose.
In contrast, we previously reported that suvorexant decreases CSF pT181/T181.

In CSF, every FDR-significant pathway at both hours 16 and 24 was enriched among proteins that increased in response to orexin antagonism; no pathway was significantly decreased centrally at either time point.

The CSF signature at hour 16 consisted of increased RNA and nucleotide binding, translation, cytoskeletal organization, cadherin and phosphatidylinositol binding, guanyl-nucleotide and G-protein modules, and KEGG endocytosis; at hour 24 only RNA binding remained significant.

In plasma, hour 16 was dominated by hepatic and catabolic metabolism pathways, and hour 24 carried the great majority of the study's significant terms, comprising translation and RNA handling, nucleotide metabolism, ubiquitin-proteasome and autophagic catabolism, endosomal and multivesicular body sorting, cytoskeletal organization and chaperone-mediated folding, together with a smaller set of significantly decreased terms covering cytokine and receptor-ligand signaling, serine protease activity and extracellular matrix constituents.

The divergent CSF and plasma pT181/T181 trajectories are consistent with altered intercompartmental handling of phosphorylated tau, but the present data cannot distinguish selective CNS-to-blood export from altered peripheral clearance, differential tau processing, assay-related effects, or compartment-specific changes in phosphorylation.
We hypothesize that selective export from the central to the peripheral compartment is one mechanism to explain the increase in plasma pT181/T181.

The absence of a significant effect on plasma Aβ40, Aβ42, or unphosphorylated T181 and T217 argues against a simple increase in bulk transfer of CNS-derived species into blood since a clearance effect of that kind should also affect Aβ and unphosphorylated tau.

Further, the CSF pool of tau is approximately 20-fold more concentrated than the plasma pool. 24 Therefore, exporting a smaller relative fraction of CSF p-tau would be predicted to increase the plasma p-tau pool by a greater relative amount.

text.text: There are alternative hypotheses, however, including reduced peripheral proteolytic capacity for phosphorylated tau and/or central versus peripheral differences in kinase engagement with tau.

Both alternatives are difficult to assess since the proteomic data does not measure activity or concentration, although pathways that would support these hypotheses also do not align with the biomarker changes.

Multiple pathways associated with the ubiquitin-proteasome-chaperone system that degrades tau were also enriched at hour 24 in plasma but not at hour 16 or in CSF: modification-dependent protein catabolic process (GO:0019941), ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process (GO:0006511), regulation of proteasomal protein catabolic process (GO:0061136), and others.

DORAs, such as suvorexant and lemborexant, reduce pT181/T181 in human CSF 12 and tau phosphorylation in transgenic mice. 10 In mice, lemborexant decreased phosphorylated tau and tau-mediated neurodegeneration via protein kinase A (PKA) and microglia changes. 10 The CSF signature, however, does not contain pathways directly associated with tau phosphorylation that reached FDR < 0.05 at either time point.

text.text: This study represents one of the first attempts to measure the effect of DORAs on plasma AD biomarkers and to map the proteomic effects of orexin antagonism across CSF and plasma in cognitively unimpaired adults.
However, there are several important limitations.
Suvorexant-mediated changes were measured over hours in a small cohort of cognitively unimpaired middle-aged adults.
We identified several pathway-level changes significant after FDR-correction despite the limited power to detect individual protein changes.

SomaScan and NULISA measure relative protein abundance, not activity or concentration, and both assays assess the extracellular compartment, so terms describing intracellular processes reflect the origin and annotation of the proteins detected rather than processes occurring in CSF or plasma.
Further, measurement of additional forms of phosphorylated tau in CSF and plasma as well as confirmation of proteomic changes with dedicated mass spectrometry or immunoassays are needed.

We emphasize that no published work connects orexin signaling to all of the mechanisms discussed and that the link from suvorexant to these plasma changes is inferred from the enrichment pattern and needs further testing.

Given the rapid adoption of plasma AD biomarkers for clinical care and research, factors that influence their levels, such as medications like suvorexant, must be identified and their effects on interpretation understood.

Human CSF and plasma samples from participants treated with suvorexant 20 mg or placebo from t=0 (20:00 on Day 1), t=16 (12:00 on Day 2), and t=24 (20:00 on Day 2) timepoints were assayed using the SomaScan 11K kit (SomaLogic, Boulder, CO), which is a high-scale aptamer-based proteomic platform that measures relative concentrations of ~11,000 proteins.
These timepoints were chosen to capture both the greatest AD biomarker change (hour 16) and circadian-matched comparisons (hour 24) relative to baseline.
CSF and plasma samples were available from 13 participants in the placebo group and 12 participants in the suvorexant group at hours 0 and 16.
At hour 24, there was one participant in each group without CSF available for analysis.
All CSF and plasma samples were analyzed per manufacturer's instructions.

Briefly, we input 50 μL of plasma samples and prepared in 3 separate plate wells at 40%, 1%, and 0.005% dilution, respectively, and a single 20% dilution across all CSF sample wells on the SomaScan assay plate.
Samples were hybridized into Agilent Surescan MicroArray slides and then scanned at a 5-μm resolution to detect CY3 fluorescence.
Gridding and image analysis were done using Agilent Feature Extraction v10.7.3.1.
Raw signals were standardized according to SomaScan. 44

T0) and at hour 24 versus baseline (T24 vs.
A participant-paired moderated t-test with empirical Bayes shrinkage of variance was used to identify differentially expressed proteins.
The limma package generates both nominal p-values and multiple testing-corrected adjusted p-values using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure.

Given that pathway-level genes tend to be co-regulated, proteins with nominal p < 0.05 were included in downstream pathway enrichment analyses to reduce false negative rates at the individual protein level.

text.text: Upregulated and downregulated protein gene lists based on the SomaScan data were processed through the web interface Metascape for the gene ontology, biological function, and pathway analyses.
The Metascape utilizes the well-adopted hypergeometric test to identify statistically enriched ontology terms.

Significant terms were defined as those with a minimum count of three genes and an enrichment factor more than 1.5 (i.e., the ratio between the observed counts and the counts expected by chance) at p < 0.05 or Benjamini-Hochberg FDR corrected p < 0.05.

text.text: The Metascape also uses Kappa similarity algorithm to absorb most redundancies of biological terms into representative clusters.
Clusters were named based on the most statistically significant term within the cluster.
Analysis in Metascape provided the top upregulated and downregulated gene ontology clusters with their representative enriched terms for illustration and discussion.
To capture the relationships between terms, we selected the top 15 enriched terms from each of the 20 top cluster terms and rendered them as a network plot visualized with Cytoscape.
The terms with the best p-values had no more than 15 terms per cluster and no more than 250 terms in total.

Circle node color is paired with the enriched terms that represent cluster identity (text written in the same color in the figure) and node size is proportional to the number of input genes included in the selected terms.
Terms with a Kappa similarity score > 0.3 are linked by a branch whose thickness represents the similarity score.

text.text: Finally, we use STRING and BioGrid to reveal enriched protein-protein physical interactions.
Protein interaction networks containing between 3 and 500 proteins were included and analyzed through the MCODE algorithm to identify densely connected network components.
The three best-scoring terms by p-value were retained as a functional description of the corresponding components.
Serial CSF Aβ, tau, and phospho-tau data were analyzed using general linear mixed models to account for dependencies among longitudinal measurements.
The mixed model used a compound symmetry covariance matrix and was fit using restricted maximum likelihood (REML) as implemented in GraphPad Prism 8.0.
Intervention group, time of day, and intervention × time interaction were treated as fixed effects; random intercepts and slopes accommodated individual variation.
Plasma AD biomarkers (Aβ40, Aβ42, pT181, T181, T217) were analyzed using the same mixed model framework.
Two-sided t-tests were used to test for group differences in individual proteins measured by SomaScan and NULISA.
For SomaScan proteomic analyses, differential expression was performed using the limma package in R with a participant-paired moderated t-test and empirical Bayes shrinkage of variance.
Multiple testing correction was applied using the Benjamini-Hochberg FDR procedure.
Individual proteins with nominal p < 0.05 were used for downstream pathway enrichment analyses.
